title: What is the Sharpe Ratio?
subtitle: Measuring return earned per unit of risk taken on
openingQuestion: Fund A returns 20%/year with 25% volatility. Fund B returns 12%/year with 10% volatility. The risk-free rate is 3%. Which fund has the higher Sharpe Ratio?
openingOptions: Fund A, because its absolute return is higher
Fund B - Sharpe A = (20-3)/25 = 0.68; Sharpe B = (12-3)/10 = 0.9 - B is more efficient per unit of risk despite a lower absolute return
Cannot be calculated without more information
explanation: Sharpe Ratio = (portfolio return − risk-free rate) / portfolio standard deviation. This is a measure of the excess return (over a risk-free asset) earned for EACH unit of risk taken on. A higher Sharpe Ratio means more efficient risk management, not simply a higher absolute return.

diagram.label: = Sharpe Ratio (return per unit of risk)

realWorldExample.description: Fund analysts always compare Sharpe Ratios instead of just looking at absolute return - a fund earning 30%/year with extreme volatility can be less attractive than a fund steadily earning 15%/year, once you account for the risk taken on.

quiz.question: Why can comparing only absolute return between two funds be misleading?
options: Because absolute return hasn't had the investor's income tax deducted
Because absolute return doesn't account for the fund's management fee
Because the two funds may use different measurement periods within the year
Because the same level of return can be achieved with very different risk
quiz.explanation: This is exactly the value of risk-adjusted return metrics like the Sharpe Ratio: they force you to consider BOTH return AND risk at once. A hedge fund earning 40%/year through extreme leverage isn't necessarily 'better' than an index fund steadily earning 12%/year - the Sharpe Ratio allows a fairer comparison.

quiz.question: A fund has a negative Sharpe Ratio (its return is lower than even the risk-free rate). What does this say about that fund's performance?
options: The investor took on risk yet received less than a risk-free deposit
The fund lost principal throughout the entire measured period
The fund has below-average market volatility
The ratio was calculated wrong, since a Sharpe Ratio can never be negative
quiz.explanation: A negative Sharpe Ratio is a serious warning sign: it means the investor accepted volatility but received a return LOWER than taking no risk at all (the risk-free rate) - essentially "paying" for a worse outcome than the safest option.

quiz.question: A fund returns 14%, the risk-free rate is 4%, standard deviation is 20%. What is the Sharpe Ratio?
options: 0.7 (= 14% ÷ 20%, forgetting to subtract the risk-free rate)
0.5 (= (14% − 4%) ÷ 20% standard deviation)
2.0 (= (14% − 4%) ÷ 5%, the wrong standard deviation)
10 (= 14% − 4%, without dividing by standard deviation)
quiz.explanation: Sharpe = (return − risk-free rate) / standard deviation = 10/20 = 0.5. Each unit of volatility endured buys back half a unit of excess return - a modest figure, generally considered acceptable from around 1.0 up.

quiz.question: Fund A: returns 18%, volatility 30%. Fund B: returns 12%, volatility 10%. Risk-free rate 3%. Which is more efficient?
options: Both are equivalent once risk is fully accounted for
A, because its absolute return is far higher than B's
B, since its Sharpe of 0.9 beats A's 0.5
Cannot be compared since the two funds hold different asset types
quiz.explanation: A gives a Sharpe of (18−3)/30 = 0.5; B gives (12−3)/10 = 0.9. B earns less but gets back nearly twice as much per unit of risk - and with leverage, B could be scaled up to beat A at the same risk level.

quiz.question: What is a limitation of the Sharpe Ratio?
options: It needs at least ten years of data to be calculated
It only applies to all-stock portfolios
It completely ignores the risk-free rate in its formula
It penalizes upside volatility just as much as downside volatility
quiz.explanation: Standard deviation treats a month that's up 10% exactly the same as a month that's down 10%, even though the investor only fears the latter. This is why the Sortino Ratio was created - it only counts downside volatility.

keyTakeaways: Sharpe Ratio = (return − risk-free rate) / standard deviation
Measures return efficiency per unit of risk, not just absolute return
The standard metric for comparing performance across different investment funds

practicePrompt.question: Fund A returns 15%/year with 20% volatility (standard deviation); Fund B returns 10%/year with only 8% volatility. The risk-free rate is 4%. Which fund has better risk-adjusted performance (a higher Sharpe Ratio)?
options: Fund A is better because its absolute return is higher, without needing to consider standard deviation
Both funds have equal risk-adjusted performance since both beat the risk-free rate
Fund B is worse since its absolute return is lower than Fund A's
practicePrompt.explanation: Sharpe Ratio = (return − risk-free rate) / standard deviation. B has a higher Sharpe Ratio (0.75) than A (0.55) despite a lower absolute return - this is why the Sharpe Ratio matters more than absolute return when comparing fund performance, since it accounts for the risk taken on to achieve that return.

summary.keyIdea: Sharpe Ratio = (return − risk-free rate) / standard deviation
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Measures return efficiency per unit of risk, not just absolute return

application.title: Calculate a fund's Sharpe Ratio
application.message: The lesson already worked a real example calculating VESAF's Sharpe Ratio numerator (excess return ~18.8 percentage points) - see the 'Real example' section above. Now look up that fund's standard deviation yourself to complete the calculation.
application.secondary: Comparing it against another fund of the same type will show you which one manages risk more effectively.

sections.text: The Sharpe Ratio answers the question: "at what cost of risk was this return achieved?" **Formula:** Sharpe Ratio = (portfolio return − risk-free rate) / portfolio standard deviation. The higher the ratio, the more efficiently the portfolio earns per unit of risk taken on - not simply a higher absolute return.
Why absolute return alone isn't enough

Comparing absolute return between two funds can be misleading because it ignores the level of risk taken on. A hedge fund earning 40%/year through extreme leverage isn't necessarily "better" than an index fund steadily earning 12%/year. **Example:** if Fund A returns 15% with a 10% standard deviation and the risk-free rate is 3%, Sharpe = (15-3)/10 = 1.2. Fund B returns 30% but with a 35% standard deviation, Sharpe = (30-3)/35 ≈ 0.77. Despite the lower absolute return, Fund A is more efficient once risk is accounted for.
A negative Sharpe Ratio is a serious signal

When the Sharpe Ratio is negative (return lower than even the risk-free rate), it means the fund performed worse than simply holding a risk-free asset - the investor accepted volatility but got back an outcome even worse than the safest option, effectively "paying" for a worse result.

items: Sharpe Ratio = (return − risk-free rate) / standard deviation
Compares risk-adjusted return, not just absolute return
The higher the Sharpe, the better the return efficiency per unit of risk
A negative Sharpe: the fund performed worse than a risk-free asset - a strong warning sign

sections.text: Real example: estimating VESAF's Sharpe Ratio

items: Reference risk-free yield: the 10-year government bond at about 4.11%/year

Excess return = 22.9% - 4.11% ≈ 18.8 percentage points - this is the Sharpe Ratio's numerator; the denominator is the fund's standard deviation (its volatility level), which you need to look up yourself on the fund's factsheet since it changes over time

sections.label: The full formula to complete yourself
sections.text: Sharpe Ratio = (fund return - risk-free yield) / fund standard deviation. Look up the "Standard Deviation" figure on the fund's factsheet (usually published annually) to complete the calculation with the actual figures for the fund you're interested in.

lines: A high return alone tells you nothing - you have to divide it by the risk taken on to know who is genuinely managing well.
